about: THINGS SAID (Design/content/BRIEF.md, the task 'things said', 4 Oct 2026): short things said aboard and in harbours, 793-1066: weather lore, proverbs, jokes of the period's own kind, riddling questions, complaints, blessings, curses and boasts. A draft in the game's own file, for the user to overwrite. Each saying has: id; kind (one of 'kinds'); text (a line break is a verse line); answer (riddles only); people (the people ids of encounters/npc_roles_793.json who would say it, or 'any'); who (the sort of speaker, where it matters); when (plain words: a season, weather, a place or a mood, or empty); cond (only where the moment is one the engine can test, in the condition grammar of Cond.cs: month, fog, storm, ice, feast, fast, moored, under_way); source; real (false = invented in the period's manner, true = a real saying of the time or one told of it); from and to (the years between which it can be said, where it hangs on an event); text_id (the chest text in texts_793.json it is drawn from); told_later (true = written down after 1066 of this time, as texts_793.json marks toldLater); check (true = the source line carries a (?): quoted or rendered from memory and still to be checked against a printed text). WHAT IS QUOTED WORD FOR WORD, from public-domain translations checked against the printed texts on 4 Oct 2026: Hávamál and the other Eddic lays in H. A. Bellows's English (1923; his caesura mark is left out and his own stanza numbers are given, which run one ahead of the chest's from stanza 76 on); Kuno Meyer's Irish verse, the Triads of Ireland and the Instructions of King Cormac (Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911); the scribes' notes in the margins of the St Gall Priscian in the English of Stokes and Strachan (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II, 1903); Notker the Stammerer in A. J. Grant's English (1907); Rimbert in C. H. Robinson's (1921); Gestumblindi's riddles in Vigfusson and York Powell's (1883, already in the chest); the Latin Bible's sayings in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner, 1750). WHAT IS THE GAME'S OWN RENDERING from the original, in plain words, because no free translation exists or the old ones are in 'thee' and 'thou': the Durham Proverbs (first printed in 1956), the Old English Maxims, the Rune Poem, Beowulf, The Wanderer and The Seafarer, the charms, Ælfric's Colloquy, Alcuin's Disputatio Pippini, the Propositiones and the Conflictus, the Latin colophons, the rune stones, and the saga sayings. The Old English and the Latin of the Propositiones and the Conflictus were read from the printed texts; the Disputatio, the Durham Proverbs after no. 25, Notker the German's proverbs and a few others were rendered from memory and carry (?) and check. WHAT IS INVENTED is marked 'invented in the period's manner' at the start of its source, with the true thing it leans on after a semicolon where there is one. Invented sayings name a king or a saint only in passing, use no word the brief forbids, and say dates by feasts and moons.

sayings.text:
Within the gates ere a man shall go,
(Full warily let him watch,)
Full long let him look about him;
For little he knows where a foe may lurk,
And sit in the seats within.
sayings.who: a careful guest
sayings.when: coming into a strange hall or a strange harbour
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 1 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Fire he needs who with frozen knees
Has come from the cold without;
Food and clothes must the farer have,
The man from the mountains come.
sayings.when: cold; coming in wet from the sea
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 3 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Wits must he have who wanders wide,
But all is easy at home;
At the witless man the wise shall wink
When among such men he sits.
sayings.who: a far-travelled man
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 5 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The knowing guest who goes to the feast,
In silent attention sits;
With his ears he hears, with his eyes he watches,
Thus wary are wise men all.
sayings.when: at a feast; in an ale-house where news is told
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 7 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A better burden may no man bear
For wanderings wide than wisdom;
It is better than wealth on unknown ways,
And in grief a refuge it gives.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 10 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A better burden may no man bear
For wanderings wide than wisdom;
Worse food for the journey he brings not afield
Than an over-drinking of ale.
sayings.when: at the ale-house, the night before sailing
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 11 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Less good there lies than most believe
In ale for mortal men;
For the more he drinks the less does man
Of his mind the mastery hold.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 12 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The sluggard believes he shall live forever,
If the fight he faces not;
But age shall not grant him the gift of peace,
Though spears may spare his life.
sayings.when: before danger; when a man hangs back
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 16 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The fool is agape when he comes to the feast,
He stammers or else is still;
But soon if he gets a drink is it seen
What the mind of the man is like.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 17 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The herds know well when home they shall fare,
And then from the grass they go;
But the foolish man his belly's measure
Shall never know aright.
sayings.when: at a feast; of a greedy man
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 21 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The witless man is awake all night,
Thinking of many things;
Care-worn he is when the morning comes,
And his woe is just as it was.
sayings.when: a bad night; a debt on the mind
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 23 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
An ignorant man thinks that all he knows,
When he sits by himself in a corner;
But never what answer to make he knows,
When others with questions come.
sayings.when: of a man who knows every price until he is asked one
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 26 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A witless man, when he meets with men,
Had best in silence abide;
For no one shall find that nothing he knows,
If his mouth is not open too much.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 27 as Bellows numbers it, the first four lines (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Often he speaks who never is still
With words that win no faith;
The babbling tongue, if a bridle it find not,
Oft for itself sings ill.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 29 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Oft should one make an early meal,
Nor fasting come to the feast;
Else he sits and chews as if he would choke,
And little is able to ask.
sayings.when: before a feast; before a long day of bargaining
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 33 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Crooked and far is the road to a foe,
Though his house on the highway be;
But wide and straight is the way to a friend,
Though far away he fare.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 34 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Forth shall one go, nor stay as a guest
In a single spot forever;
Love becomes loathing if long one sits
By the hearth in another's home.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 35 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Better a house, though a hut it be,
A man is master at home;
A pair of goats and a patched-up roof
Are better far than begging.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 36 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Away from his arms in the open field
A man should fare not a foot;
For never he knows when the need for a spear
Shall arise on the distant road.
sayings.when: going ashore in a place not known
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 38 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
If wealth a man has won for himself,
Let him never suffer in need;
Oft he saves for a foe what he plans for a friend,
For much goes worse than we wish.
sayings.when: of a man who saves and never spends
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 39 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
To his friend a man a friend shall prove,
And gifts with gifts requite;
But men shall mocking with mockery answer,
And fraud with falsehood meet.
sayings.when: after a gift; after a cheat
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 42 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Young was I once, and wandered alone,
And nought of the road I knew;
Rich did I feel when a comrade I found,
For man is man's delight.
sayings.when: meeting a known face far from home
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 47 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
My garments once in a field I gave
To a pair of carven poles;
Heroes they seemed when clothes they had,
But the naked man is nought.
sayings.when: buying cloth; of a well-dressed fool
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 49 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Hotter than fire between false friends
Does friendship five days burn;
When the sixth day comes the fire cools,
And ended is all the love.
sayings.when: of a new friend made over ale
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 51 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
No great thing needs a man to give,
Oft little will purchase praise;
With half a loaf and a half-filled cup
A friend full fast I made.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 52 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A little sand has a little sea,
And small are the minds of men;
Though all men are not equal in wisdom,
Yet half-wise only are all.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 53 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A measure of wisdom each man shall have,
But never too much let him know;
Let no man the fate before him see,
For so is he freest from sorrow.
sayings.when: when someone wants an omen read
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 56 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A brand from a brand is kindled and burned,
And fire from fire begotten;
And man by his speech is known to men,
And the stupid by their stillness.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 57 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
He must early go forth who fain the blood
Or the goods of another would get;
The wolf that lies idle shall win little meat,
Or the sleeping man success.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 58 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
He must early go forth whose workers are few,
Himself his work to seek;
Much remains undone for the morning-sleeper,
For the swift is wealth half won.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 59 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
When the eagle comes to the ancient sea,
He snaps and hangs his head;
So is a man in the midst of a throng,
Who few to speak for him finds.
sayings.when: a stranger at the thing, with no one to speak for him
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 62 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.when: coming late to a fair, or too early
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 66 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
To their homes men would bid me hither and yon,
If at meal-time I needed no meat,
Or would hang two hams in my true friend's house,
Where only one I had eaten.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 67 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Fire for men is the fairest gift,
And power to see the sun;
Health as well, if a man may have it,
And a life not stained with sin.
sayings.when: at a fire after a cold passage
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 68 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
It is better to live than to lie a corpse,
The live man catches the cow;
I saw flames rise for the rich man's pyre,
And before his door he lay dead.
sayings.when: after a loss; after a wreck that left the men alive
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 70 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The lame rides a horse, the handless is herdsman,
The deaf in battle is bold;
The blind man is better than one that is burned,
No good can come of a corpse.
sayings.when: of a hurt man who can still work
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 71 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A son is better, though late he be born,
And his father to death have fared;
Memory-stones seldom stand by the road
Save when kinsman honors his kin.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 72 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Two make a battle, the tongue slays the head;
In each furry coat a fist I look for.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 73 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
He welcomes the night whose fare is enough,
(Short are the yards of a ship,)
Uneasy are autumn nights;
Full oft does the weather change in a week,
And more in a month's time.
sayings.when: autumn; the last passages of the year
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 74 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Among Fitjung's sons saw I well-stocked folds,--
Now bear they the beggar's staff;
Wealth is as swift as a winking eye,
Of friends the falsest it is.
sayings.when: of a rich house come down
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 76 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Cattle die, and kinsmen die,
And so one dies one's self;
But a noble name will never die,
If good renown one gets.
sayings.when: at a burial; of a good name
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 77 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Give praise to the day at evening, to a woman on her pyre,
To a weapon which is tried, to a maid at wed lock,
To ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk.
sayings.when: when a venture is praised before it is home
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 81 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.when: a gale in harbour; a fair wind
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 82 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The love of women fickle of will
Is like starting o'er ice with a steed unshod,
A two-year-old restive and little tamed,
Or steering a rudderless ship in a storm,
Or, lame, hunting reindeer on slippery rocks.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 90 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
The head alone knows what dwells near the heart,
A man knows his mind alone;
No sickness is worse to one who is wise
Than to lack the longed-for joy.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 95 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
For brambles grow and waving grass
On the rarely trodden road.
sayings.when: of a friend not visited, a port not called at
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 119 as Bellows numbers it, the last two lines (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Oft scarcely he knows who sits in the house
What kind is the man who comes;
None so good is found that faults he has not,
Nor so wicked that nought he is worth.
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 133 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Scorn not ever the gray-haired singer,
Oft do the old speak good;
sayings.when: when an old man sings or gives advice
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 134 as Bellows numbers it, lines 4 and 5 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A ninth I know, if need there comes
To shelter my ship on the flood;
The wind I calm upon the waves,
And the sea I put to sleep.
sayings.who: a man who says he knows the old songs
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 155 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
A seventh I know, if I see in flames
The hall o'er my comrades' heads;
It burns not so wide that I will not quench it,
I know that song to sing.
sayings.who: a man who says he knows the old songs
sayings.when: of fire in a hall or a town
sayings.source: Hávamál, stanza 153 as Bellows numbers it (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); written down in the 13th century

sayings.text:
Who yonder rides on Rævil's steeds,
O'er towering waves and waters wild?
The sail-horses all with sweat are dripping,
Nor can the sea-steeds the gale withstand.
sayings.answer: Ships in a gale: Rævil was a sea-king, and his steeds are ships.
sayings.who: a man on a headland, hailing a ship
sayings.source: Reginsmol 16 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923)

sayings.text:
Many the signs, if men but knew,
That are good for the swinging of swords;
It is well, methinks, if the warrior meets
A raven black on his road.
sayings.when: of omens, before a fight or a venture
sayings.source: Reginsmol 20 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923)
Reginsmol 25, the first three lines (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923)

sayings.text:
Hail, day! Hail, sons of day!
And night and her daughter now!
Look on us here with loving eyes,
That waiting we victory win.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.source: Sigrdrifumol 2 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923)

sayings.text:
Hail to the gods! Ye goddesses, hail,
And all the generous earth!
Give to us wisdom and goodly speech,
And healing hands, life-long.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.source: Sigrdrifumol 3 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923)

sayings.who: a rune-cutter
sayings.source: Sigrdrifumol 9 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); the 'thou' is Bellows's

sayings.text: What kind of a peasant is yon, that calls o'er the bay?
sayings.who: a ferryman
sayings.source: Harbarthsljoth 2 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923): the ferryman to Thor

sayings.when: asking a passage and offering to pay in food
sayings.source: Harbarthsljoth 3, lines 2 to 4 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923): Thor to the ferryman

sayings.text:
The oak must have what it shaves from another;
In such things each for himself.
sayings.when: of taking what another has lost
sayings.source: Harbarthsljoth 22, the first two lines (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923); the same saying is in Grettis saga

sayings.text: No heel-biter am I, in truth, like an old leather shoe in spring.
sayings.source: Harbarthsljoth 35 (H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923)

sayings.text: Go safe, come back safe, and be safe on the way.
sayings.source: Vafthruthnismal 4, Frigg to Odin at his going ('Heill þú farir, heill þú aptr komir, heill þú á sinnum sér'); the game's own rendering from the Old Norse (Bellows, 1923, has 'Safe mayst thou go')

sayings.text: Patience is half of happiness.
sayings.when: waiting for a wind; waiting for a debtor
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 1 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A friend is good far or near; the nearer is the more use.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 2 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: In need a man finds out his friends.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 3 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: No man has too many friends.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 4 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: He begs in front of his friend who complains of his own want.
sayings.when: of a man who talks of his losses
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 5 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: It is a good year when the dog gives to the raven.
sayings.when: a fat year; a good harvest
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 6 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Treasure often lies in a sooty bag.
sayings.when: of a shabby boat with a rich cargo
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 7 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Sometimes men are thirstiest after mead.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 8 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: It is for the dear one that the longing is worst.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 9 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: 'Now it is up to the pig,' said the churl on the boar's back.
sayings.when: when the matter is out of your hands: a tide, a toll man, a king
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 10 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: 'All the same, I would not trust you, though you walked well,' said the man who saw a witch walking on her head.
sayings.when: of a seller whose goods look too good
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 11 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A man does as he is when he may do as he likes.
sayings.when: of a man newly rich, or newly master
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 14 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: He is blind in both eyes who does not look with his heart.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 17 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Those do not quarrel who are not together.
sayings.when: a quarrel aboard, in a boat too small for one
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 18 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: It does no good to tell every truth, nor to blame every wrong.
sayings.when: at the toll; before a reeve
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 19 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: If you speak well, do as well after.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 20 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Truth makes itself known.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 21 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A coward can do one thing only: be afraid.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 22 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A man should be neither too soon afraid nor too soon glad.
sayings.when: a strange sail; a good price heard of
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 23 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The man who has done wrong has need of peace.
sayings.when: of a man who has run to a church
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 24 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Better to try a hundred places than to bear a hundred shames.
sayings.when: leaving a port where you were cheated
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs 25 (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The fuller the cup, the more carefully it must be carried.
sayings.when: a full hold; a full cup
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Swa fulre fæt swa hit mann sceal fægror beran'

sayings.text: He loses his thanks who does a kindness to a worthless man.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Leana forleosaþ se þe hit lyþran deð'

sayings.text: Every gift looks back over its shoulder.
sayings.when: when a great man gives you something
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Gyfena gehwilc underbæc besihþ'

sayings.text: The whole host is bold when its leader is bold.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Eall here byþ hwæt þonne se lateow byþ hwæt'

sayings.text: He does not know the worth of sweet who has never tasted bitter.
sayings.when: after a hard passage, at a good fire
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Ne wat swetes ðanc se þe biteres ne onbyrgeð'

sayings.text: Often it is better to be loaded than overloaded.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Betere byþ oft feðre þonne oferfeðre'

sayings.text: Every trick is paid back cold.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Cræfta gehwilc byþ cealde forgolden'

sayings.text: Need teaches many things.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Seo nydþearf feala læreð'

sayings.text: He boasts little who travels far.
sayings.when: when a young man brags of his one voyage
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Hwon gelpeð se þe wide siþað'

sayings.text: Everyone who calls out wants to be heard.
sayings.when: a hail across the water; a hawker in the market
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Ciggendra gehwilc wile þæt hine man gehere'

sayings.text: He must not mourn for the horse who means to run down the hart.
sayings.when: driving the boat hard for a market
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Ne sceall se for horse murnan se þe wile heort ofærnan'

sayings.text: No man can have his mouth full of flour and blow the fire as well.
sayings.when: when a man wants two things at once
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Ne mæg man muþ fulne melewes habban and eac fyr blawan'

sayings.text: 'It is not well anywhere,' said the man who heard the wailing in hell.
sayings.when: when every port has the same bad news
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, number not checked (?) (Durham Cathedral MS B.III.32, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered: 'Wide ne biþ wel, cwæþ se þe gehyrde on helle hriman'

sayings.text: Wind is the swiftest thing in the sky; thunder at times the loudest. The powers of Christ are great. Fate is strongest.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 3-5 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Winter is coldest; spring is frostiest and longest cold; summer is brightest with sun; autumn is most blessed, and brings men the fruits of the year that God sends them.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 5-9 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Truth is plainest, treasure dearest, and the old man wisest, who has lived through much.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 10-12 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Woe clings wonderfully fast. The clouds glide on.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 13 (reading 'wea', woe, with the manuscript) (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The mast belongs on the ship, and the sailyard hanging from it.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 24-25 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The fish in the water must breed its kind. The king in the hall must give out rings.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 27-29 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The dragon belongs in the barrow, old and proud of his treasure.
sayings.when: of a rich man who spends nothing; of an old barrow on the shore
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 26-27 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The river runs down from the hill, flood-grey.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 30-31 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The shower must come down from heaven into this world, mixed with wind.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 40-41 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The thief goes out in dark weather. The giant lives in the fen, alone in the land.
sayings.when: a dark night in harbour; fen country
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 42-43 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The sea must surge with salt; cloud and flood flow round every land.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 45-47 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The stars must shine bright in heaven, as the Maker bade them.
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 48-49 (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: God alone knows where the soul goes afterwards. No one comes back here under our roofs to tell men the truth of it.
sayings.when: at a burial; after a drowning
sayings.source: Maxims II, ll. 57-66, shortened (British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Wise men should trade sayings.
sayings.when: opening a round of riddles or sayings
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 4 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Frost must freeze, fire eat wood, earth grow, ice make a bridge, and water wear a roof.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 71-73 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: One alone unbinds the frost's fetters, God almighty. Winter must turn and good weather come again, summer hot with sun, the sea unquiet.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 74-77 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The deep way of the dead is longest secret.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 78 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A ship must be nailed, a shield bound. And dear is the welcome one to the Frisian wife when the ship stands in: his keel is come and her man is home, her own provider. She calls him in, washes his sea-stained clothes and gives him fresh ones.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 93-98 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A wife should keep faith with her man. Many are steadfast; many are curious, and love a stranger when the other is far off.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 100-102 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The seaman is long on his voyage; yet always one must look for the loved one, and wait for what cannot be hurried. He comes home, if he lives, unless the sea holds him.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 103-106 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The trading man, when he comes in from sailing, has the use of wood and water once a lodging is granted him; he buys food if he needs more, before he grows too weak.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 107-110 (the sense of the first line is disputed) (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: He is sick who eats too seldom.
sayings.when: of a man who will not eat at sea
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 111 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A strong mind must be steered. The storm often brings the sea into grim moods.
sayings.when: a storm coming; a hot temper aboard
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 50-51 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The sea is calm when the wind does not wake it. So peoples are at peace when they have settled their quarrels.
sayings.when: a calm; a quarrel made up
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 54-56 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Every mouth needs food; meals must come at their times.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 124 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A man should keep his friends on every road. Often he goes far round a town where he knows he has no sure friend.
sayings.when: choosing which port to call at
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 144-145 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The friendless, luckless man takes wolves for companions, treacherous beasts; very often that companion tears him.
sayings.when: of a man who sails with bad company
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 146-147 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A felled tree grows least.
sayings.when: of a boat laid up too long; of an idle man
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 158 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: As many men as there are on earth, so many minds; each has a mind of his own.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 167-168 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: He longs the less who knows many songs, or can play the harp with his hands; he has his gift of music, which God gave him.
sayings.when: a long watch; a long winter
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 169-171 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Wretched is he who must live alone; fate has laid it on him to dwell friendless.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 172-173 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Two should sit at the board until their trouble slides from them, forget their hard lot, and have their sport at the game.
sayings.when: windbound; a board game in harbour
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 181-182 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Seldom in a broad ship, unless she runs under sail, does a weary man row against the wind. Very often they call him a shirker, so that he loses heart, and his oar dries on the gunwale.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 184-186 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Woden made idols; the Almighty made glory, the wide heavens.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 132-133 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The ready man must go, the doomed man die.
sayings.when: setting out on a bad day
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 27 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A tree on earth must lose its leaves; the branches mourn.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 25-26 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: God may give goods to the lucky man and take them back again.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 155-156 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Happy is he who thrives in his own country; wretched he whose friends fail him.
sayings.source: Maxims I, ll. 37 (Exeter Book, written c. 970); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Wealth is a comfort to every man; yet each must give it freely if he wants good standing before the Lord.
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 1-3 (the rune feoh, wealth); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Riding is easy for a man in the hall, and very hard for him who sits on a strong horse over the mile-long roads.
sayings.when: of a man who talks of journeys from the bench
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 13-15 (the rune rad, riding); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Hail is the whitest of grains; it whirls from heaven's height, the wind's showers toss it, and then it turns to water.
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 25-26 (the rune hægl, hail); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Need is tight on the breast; yet it often turns to help and healing for the sons of men, if they heed it in time.
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 27-28 (the rune nyd, need); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Ice is very cold and slippery beyond measure; it glitters clear as glass, most like to gems; a floor made by frost, fair to see.
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 29-31 (the rune is, ice); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: A good year is the hope of men, when God, the holy king of heaven, lets the earth give bright fruits to rich and poor.
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 32-34 (the rune ger, the year's harvest); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The sun is always a hope to seamen when they ferry over the fish's bath, until the sea-horse brings them to land.
sayings.when: the sun breaking through at sea
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 45-47 (the rune sigel, sun); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Tir is one of the signs: it keeps faith well with princes, it is always on its course over the mists of night, and it never fails.
sayings.who: a steersman
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 48-50 (the rune tir, a star or sign to steer by); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The sea seems endless to men if they must venture out in a tippy boat, and the waves frighten them badly, and the sea-horse does not heed its bridle.
sayings.when: rough water in a small boat
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 63-66 (the rune lagu, water); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: The oak feeds the pigs that feed men; often it travels over the gannet's bath, and the sea finds out whether the oak keeps faith.
sayings.who: a shipwright
sayings.when: of a new ship on her first passage
sayings.source: The Old English Rune Poem, ll. 77-80 (the rune ac, oak); the game's own rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: Fate goes always as it must.
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 455; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: Fate often spares the man not yet doomed, when his courage holds.
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 572-573; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: A sharp man with a shield, who thinks well, must know the difference between words and deeds.
sayings.who: a coast-warden or a reeve
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 287-289 (the Danish coast-warden to Beowulf); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: Better for a man to avenge his friend than to mourn much.
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 1384-1385; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: Each of us must wait for the end of life in this world; let him who can win a good name before death.
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 1386-1388; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: Far countries are best visited by the man who is himself worth something.
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 1838-1839; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: Death is better for any man than a life of shame.
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 2890-2891; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: He who is long in this world, in these days of strife, will live through much that he loves and much that he hates.
sayings.who: an old hand
sayings.source: Beowulf, ll. 1060-1062; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has J. L. Hall's of 1892)

sayings.text: Fate is wholly fixed.
sayings.source: The Wanderer, ll. 5 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has E. H. Hickey's of 1881)

sayings.text: A man cannot grow wise before he has had his share of winters in the world.
sayings.who: an old hand
sayings.source: The Wanderer, ll. 64-65 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has E. H. Hickey's of 1881)

sayings.text: A wise man must be patient: not too hot of heart, nor too quick to speak, nor too fearful, nor too glad, nor too greedy for goods, and never too keen to boast before he knows for sure.
sayings.source: The Wanderer, ll. 65-69, shortened (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has E. H. Hickey's of 1881)

sayings.text: Here goods are lent, here friends are lent, here man is lent, here kin is lent.
sayings.source: The Wanderer, ll. 108-109 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has E. H. Hickey's of 1881)

sayings.text: The man whose lot is fairest on land does not know how I, worn with care, lived a winter on the ice-cold sea.
sayings.when: winter at sea; to a man who has never left the land
sayings.source: The Seafarer, ll. 12-15 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has L. L. Iddings's of 1902)

sayings.text: At times I had the swan's song for my pleasure, the gannet's cry and the curlew's call for the laughter of men, the gull's singing for mead.
sayings.source: The Seafarer, ll. 19-22 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has L. L. Iddings's of 1902)

sayings.text: The shadow of night grew dark; it snowed from the north; frost bound the ground; hail fell on the earth, the coldest of grains.
sayings.source: The Seafarer, ll. 31-33 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has L. L. Iddings's of 1902)

sayings.text: He has no heart for the harp, nor for the taking of rings, nor joy in a woman, nor hope in the world, nor thought of anything but the rolling of the waves; he has always a longing who sets out on the sea.
sayings.when: of a man who cannot stay ashore
sayings.source: The Seafarer, ll. 44-47 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has L. L. Iddings's of 1902)

sayings.text: The woods take blossom, the towns grow fair, the fields brighten, the world quickens: all of it urges the eager heart to the voyage.
sayings.when: spring; the boats going down to the water
sayings.source: The Seafarer, ll. 48-52 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has L. L. Iddings's of 1902)

sayings.text: The cuckoo warns with its sad voice; summer's watchman sings, and bodes bitter sorrow in the breast.
sayings.source: The Seafarer, ll. 53-55 (Exeter Book); the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has L. L. Iddings's of 1902)

sayings.text: The slow man often puts off glory and every victory; and so he dies alone.
sayings.when: when a man keeps putting off his sailing
sayings.source: An Old English proverb quoted in a letter of the Boniface collection, written between 757 and 786 ('Oft daedlata dome foreldit, sigisitha gahuem; suuyltit thi ana'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: When the leader weakens, the whole host is badly hindered.
sayings.when: of a weak master or a weak ealdorman
sayings.source: A saying quoted in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under 1003 ('Ðonne se heretoga wacað þonne bið eall se here swiðe gehindred'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Hot grows cold, white grows dirty, dear grows hateful, light grows dark.
sayings.source: The Old English and Latin proverbs of British Library Cotton Faustina A.x, 11th century ('Hat acolað, hwit asolað, leof alaðaþ, leoht aðystrað'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Everything grows old that is not eternal.
sayings.source: The Old English and Latin proverbs of British Library Cotton Faustina A.x, 11th century ('Æghwæt forealdað þæs þe ece ne byð'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Before the journey that none can avoid, no man is so wise that he need not think, before he goes, what good or evil his soul will be judged for after his death-day.
sayings.who: a monk
sayings.when: at a deathbed; before a dangerous passage
sayings.source: Bede's Death Song, 735, in the Northumbrian of Cuthbert's letter on Bede's death; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: A man's life is like the flight of a sparrow through the hall in winter: in at one door and out at the other, from the winter into the winter again.
sayings.who: a monk or a thoughtful man
sayings.when: winter, by the fire in a hall
sayings.source: After Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.13 (731): the counsellor's speech to King Edwin; the game's own short telling, not a translation

sayings.text: The old name of this month is Three Milkings, because the cattle were then milked three times a day.
sayings.when: the month after Easter month, when the grass is rich
sayings.source: After Bede, De temporum ratione ch. 15 (725), on the English months (Thrimilchi); the game's own telling

sayings.text: The old people counted winter from the full moon of this month, and called it Winter Full Moon.
sayings.when: the first full moon of winter
sayings.source: After Bede, De temporum ratione ch. 15 (725), on the English months (Winterfilleth); the game's own telling

sayings.text: The old name of this month is Blood Month, because the cattle that were to be killed were then given to the gods.
sayings.source: After Bede, De temporum ratione ch. 15 (725), on the English months (Blodmonath); the game's own telling

sayings.text: Fierce March comes through the world decked with rime, in showers of hail.
sayings.when: the month of the spring gales
sayings.source: The Old English Menologium, ll. 35-37, late 10th century ('hrime gehyrsted hagolscurum færð geond middangeard Martius reðe'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: I ask the God of victories, by God's mercy, for a good journey, and a mild and light wind to the shores.
sayings.source: The Old English Journey Charm (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 41, 11th century), ll. 33-35; the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Forth I go: may I meet with friends.
sayings.source: The Old English Journey Charm (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 41, 11th century: 'Forð ic gefare, frind ic gemete'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Out, little spear, if you are in here!
sayings.who: a man or woman who knows the old cures
sayings.when: a sudden stitch or cramp at the oar
sayings.source: The Old English charm against a sudden stitch (British Library Harley 585, c. 1000: 'Ut, lytel spere, gif her inne sie'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Bethlehem is the name of the town where Christ was born; it is famed over all the earth. So may this deed become known among men, through the holy cross of Christ.
sayings.when: when goods have been stolen in harbour
sayings.source: The Old English charm for stolen cattle (Metrical Charm 5, in 11th-century manuscripts); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Be well, earth, mother of men.
sayings.source: The Old English field blessing (British Library Cotton Caligula A.vii, 11th century: 'Hal wes þu, folde, fira modor'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Be whole.
sayings.source: The Old English greeting 'wes hal' (so Beowulf to Hrothgar, l. 407: 'Wæs þu, Hroðgar, hal'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: I want to sell here dearer than I bought there, so that I get some profit to feed myself, my wife and my son.
sayings.who: a merchant
sayings.when: asked why he sells dearer than he bought
sayings.source: Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 1000, the merchant; the game's own rendering from the Old English gloss as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Sometimes I suffer shipwreck with the loss of all my things, barely escaping alive.
sayings.who: a merchant
sayings.source: Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 1000, the merchant; the chest's own draft from the original (texts_793.json, aelfric_merchant)

sayings.text: I would rather catch a fish I can kill than one that with a single blow can sink or kill not only me but my companions too.
sayings.who: a fisherman
sayings.when: asked why he does not hunt whales
sayings.source: Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 1000, the fisherman; the game's own rendering from the Old English gloss as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: It is a dangerous thing to catch a whale. It is safer for me to go on the river with my boat than to go with many ships hunting whales.
sayings.who: a fisherman
sayings.source: Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 1000, the fisherman; the game's own rendering from the Old English gloss as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Ale if I have it, or water if I have no ale.
sayings.who: a ship's boy or a novice
sayings.source: Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 1000, the boy; the game's own rendering from the Old English gloss as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: I am not so rich that I can buy myself wine; and wine is not a drink for children or fools, but for the old and wise.
sayings.who: a boy or a poor man
sayings.source: Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 1000, the boy; the game's own rendering from the Old English gloss as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: It is hard work, because I am not free.
sayings.who: an unfree man: a ploughman, a porter
sayings.source: Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 1000, the ploughman; the game's own rendering from the Old English gloss as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Mind must be the harder, heart the keener, courage the greater, as our strength grows less.
sayings.who: an old fighting man
sayings.source: The Battle of Maldon (991), ll. 312-313, the old retainer Byrhtwold; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has H. W. Lumsden's of 1902)

sayings.text: Bold seamen have sent me to you, and bid me say that you must quickly send rings for your safety. It is better for you to buy off this rush of spears with tribute than for us to share so hard a battle.
sayings.who: the spokesman of a raiding fleet
sayings.source: The Battle of Maldon (991), ll. 29-33, the messenger of the fleet; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has H. W. Lumsden's of 1902)

sayings.text: Three Irishmen came to King Alfred in a boat without any oars, from Ireland, which they had left by stealth because they wished, for the love of God, to be in foreign lands, they did not care where.
sayings.when: of pilgrims who trust the wind
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under 891; the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: This year came dreadful fore-warnings over the land of the Northumbrians, terrifying the people most woefully: these were immense sheets of light rushing through the air, and whirlwinds, and fiery dragons flying across the firmament.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under 793, in the English of the chest's text (texts_793.json, chronicle_793)

sayings.text: A wonder on the wave: water turned to bone.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 69 ('Wundor wearð on wege; wæter wearð to bane'); the game's own rendering from the Old English (Thorpe's of 1842, in the chest, reads 'poison')

sayings.text: A moth ate words. It seemed to me a strange thing that a worm should swallow a man's song, a thief in the dark, and be not a whit the wiser for the words he had eaten.
sayings.who: a monk, or anyone who has seen a book
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 47; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has Thorpe's of 1842)

sayings.text: My house is not silent, and I am not loud. I am the swifter, he the more lasting; while I rest he must run on. I live in him all my life, and if we part I die.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 85; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has Thorpe's of 1842)

sayings.text: A thing came walking where men sat in council. It had one eye, two ears, two feet, twelve hundred heads, a back and a belly, two hands, arms and shoulders, one neck and two sides. Say what I am called.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 86; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has Thorpe's of 1842)

sayings.text: Often I must fight with wave and wind together, when I go to seek the ground under the water. I am strong in the fight if I lie still. Say what I am called.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 16, shortened; the game's own rendering from the Old English (the chest has Thorpe's of 1842)

sayings.text: I am a wonder, a joy to women and of use to the neighbours; I hurt no one but the one who kills me. I stand tall in a bed, and am hairy underneath. Sometimes a churl's bold daughter grips me, strips my head and shuts me in a tight place. Soon she feels it: her eye is wet.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 25; the game's own rendering from the Old English (one of the riddles with a double meaning; Thorpe left it untranslated)

sayings.text: A strange thing hangs by a man's thigh, under its master's cloak. It is stiff and hard and pierced in front. When the man lifts his tunic above the knee, he means to greet with its head the hole it has often filled before.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 44; the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered (one of the riddles with a double meaning), to check (?)

sayings.text: I have heard of something growing in a corner, swelling and standing up, lifting its cover. A proud bride took that boneless thing in her hands; a lord's daughter covered the swelling thing with her dress.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 45; the game's own rendering from the Old English as remembered (one of the riddles with a double meaning), to check (?)

sayings.text: What is a ship?
sayings.answer: A wandering house, a lodging anywhere, a traveller who leaves no tracks, a neighbour of the sand.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Navis: domus erratica, ubilibet hospitium, viator sine vestigiis, vicinus harenae'

sayings.text: What is the sea?
sayings.answer: The road of the bold, the edge of the land, the divider of countries, the lodging of rivers, the well of the rains.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Mare: audaciae via, limes terrae, divisor regionum, hospitium fluviorum, fons imbrium'

sayings.text: What are the stars?
sayings.answer: The painting of the roof, the steersmen of sailors, the grace of the night.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Stellae: pictura culminis, nautarum gubernatores, noctis decor'

sayings.text: What is the moon?
sayings.answer: The eye of the night, the giver of dew, the foreteller of storms.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Luna: oculus noctis, roris larga, praesaga tempestatum'

sayings.text: What is fog?
sayings.answer: Night in the day, and work for the eyes.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Nebula: nox in die, labor oculorum'

sayings.text: What is wind?
sayings.answer: The stirring of the air, the moving of the waters, the drying of the land.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Ventus: aeris perturbatio, mobilitas aquarum, siccitas terrae'

sayings.text: What is frost?
sayings.answer: The persecutor of plants, the destroyer of leaves, the fetter of the earth, the bridge of the waters.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Gelu: persecutio herbarum, perditor foliorum, vinculum terrae, pons aquarum'

sayings.text: What is snow?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Nix: aqua sicca'

sayings.text: What is winter?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Hiems: aestatis exul'

sayings.text: What is spring?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Ver: pictor terrae'

sayings.text: What is autumn?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Autumnus: horreum anni'

sayings.text: What is man?
sayings.answer: The bondsman of death, a traveller passing through, a guest in the place.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Homo: mancipium mortis, transiens viator, loci hospes'

sayings.text: How is man placed?
sayings.answer: Like a lantern in the wind.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Quomodo positus est homo? Ut lucerna in vento'

sayings.text: What is sleep?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Somnus: mortis imago'

sayings.text: What is a word?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Verbum: proditor animi'

sayings.text: What is the tongue?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Lingua: flagellum aeris'

sayings.text: What makes bitter things sweet?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Quid est quod amarum dulce facit? Fames'

sayings.text: What keeps a man from growing tired?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Quid est quod hominem lassum non fieri facit? Lucrum'

sayings.text: What is the waking man's sleep?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?): 'Quid est vigilanti somnus? Spes'

sayings.text: I saw the dead give birth to the living, and the anger of the living ate up the dead.
sayings.answer: Fire, from dry wood rubbed on wood.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: I saw a guest running with his house; he was silent, and the house made the noise.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: I saw a woman flying, with an iron beak, a wooden body and a feathered tail, carrying death.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Who is it that is not, and has a name, and answers anyone who calls?
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: What is a silent messenger?
sayings.answer: The one I hold in my hand: your letter.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.when: handing over a letter to be carried
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Three there were: one never born and once dead; one once born and never dead; one once born and twice dead.
sayings.who: a monk, a priest or a schoolboy of the court
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino, c. 790-800 (Patrologia Latina 101, cols 975-980); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: A man had to take a wolf, a goat and a bundle of cabbages over a river, and the only boat he could find would carry him and one of them. He was told to bring them all over unharmed. How did he do it?
sayings.answer: He took the goat over and came back; took the wolf over and brought the goat back; took the cabbages over; and went back last for the goat.
sayings.who: a schoolman; a ferryman who has heard it from one
sayings.source: Propositiones ad acuendos iuvenes 18, ascribed to Alcuin, c. 800; the game's own rendering from the Latin

sayings.text: A man and his wife each weigh as much as a loaded cart, and their two children weigh a cartload between them. The boat will carry one cartload and no more. How do they cross without sinking her?
sayings.answer: The two children cross and one brings the boat back; the mother crosses and the other child brings it back; the two children cross and one brings it back; the father crosses and the other child brings it back; then both children cross.
sayings.who: a schoolman; a ferryman who has heard it from one
sayings.source: Propositiones ad acuendos iuvenes 19, ascribed to Alcuin, c. 800; the game's own rendering from the Latin

sayings.text: An ox ploughs all day. How many footprints does he leave in the last furrow?
sayings.answer: None: the plough comes behind him and covers them.
sayings.who: a schoolman
sayings.source: Propositiones ad acuendos iuvenes 14, ascribed to Alcuin, c. 800; the game's own rendering from the Latin

sayings.text: A dealer wants a hundred pigs for a hundred pennies. A boar costs ten pennies, a sow five, and two piglets one penny. How many of each must he buy?
sayings.answer: One boar, nine sows and ninety piglets.
sayings.who: a schoolman; a dealer
sayings.source: Propositiones ad acuendos iuvenes 5, ascribed to Alcuin, c. 800; the game's own rendering from the Latin

sayings.text: A man on the road met some others and said: I wish there were as many of you again, and half of the half of that, and half of that again; then with me you would be a hundred. How many did he meet?
sayings.who: a schoolman
sayings.source: Propositiones ad acuendos iuvenes 2, ascribed to Alcuin, c. 800; the game's own rendering from the Latin

sayings.text: A swallow asked a snail to dinner a league away, and the snail could walk no more than an inch a day. He was two hundred and forty-six years and two hundred and ten days on the road.
sayings.who: a schoolman
sayings.source: Propositiones ad acuendos iuvenes 1, with its answer, ascribed to Alcuin, c. 800; the game's own rendering from the Latin

sayings.text: Let the cuckoo not come; let him sleep in his dark cave. He always brings hunger with him.
sayings.when: the hungry spring, when the cuckoo is first heard
sayings.source: Conflictus Veris et Hiemis, ascribed to Alcuin (d. 804); the game's own rendering from the Latin: Winter speaks ('non veniat cuculus, nigris sed dormiat antris; iste famem secum semper portare suescit')

sayings.text: Let the cuckoo not come: he brings work, doubles the wars, breaks off the rest we love and stirs up everything; sea and land are put to labour.
sayings.when: the start of the sailing and fighting season
sayings.source: Conflictus Veris et Hiemis, ascribed to Alcuin (d. 804); the game's own rendering from the Latin: Winter speaks ('generat quia forte labores, proelia congeminat, requiem disiungit amatam, omnia disturbat; pelagi terraeque laborant')

sayings.text: I have riches, I have glad feasts, sweet rest, and a hot fire in the house. The cuckoo knows none of this.
sayings.source: Conflictus Veris et Hiemis, ascribed to Alcuin (d. 804); the game's own rendering from the Latin: Winter speaks ('Sunt mihi divitiae, sunt et convivia laeta, est requies dulcis, calidus est ignis in aede')

sayings.text: Let the cuckoo come with flowers in his beak: he serves the honey, builds the houses and sails the quiet waves.
sayings.source: Conflictus Veris et Hiemis, ascribed to Alcuin (d. 804); the game's own rendering from the Latin: Spring speaks ('Ore ferat flores cuculus, et mella ministrat, aedificatque domus, placidas et navigat undas')

sayings.text: What has Ingeld to do with Christ? The house is narrow; it cannot hold them both.
sayings.who: a churchman
sayings.when: when a harper sings of the old kings at a priests' table
sayings.source: Alcuin, letter of 797 to a bishop he calls Speratus (Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Epistolae IV, no. 124: 'Quid Hinieldus cum Christo?'); the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Never before has such a terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a heathen people, nor was it thought that such a voyage could be made.
sayings.who: a churchman
sayings.source: Alcuin to King Æthelred of Northumbria, 793; the chest's own draft from the Latin (texts_793.json, alcuin_793)

sayings.text: They that go down to the sea in ships, doing business in the great waters: These have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.when: at sea; in a seamen's church
sayings.source: Psalm 106:23-24, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: They mount up to the heavens, and they go down to the depths: their soul pined away with evils. They were troubled, and reeled like a drunken man; and all their wisdom was swallowed up.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Psalm 106:26-27, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: And he turned the storm into a breeze: and its waves were still. And they rejoiced because they were still: and he brought them to the haven which they wished for.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Psalm 106:29-30, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: When it is evening, you say, It will be fair weather, for the sky is red. And in the morning: Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and lowering.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Matthew 16:2-3, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: When you see a cloud rising from the west, presently you say: A shower is coming: and so it happeneth: And when ye see the south wind blow, you say: There will be heat: and it cometh to pass.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Luke 12:54-55, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: He that observeth the wind, shall not sow: and he that considereth the clouds, shall never reap.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.when: to a master who waits too long for perfect weather
sayings.source: Ecclesiastes 11:4, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: It is nought, it is nought, saith every buyer: and when he is gone away, then he will boast.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Proverbs 20:14, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord: and a just weight is his will.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Proverbs 11:1, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: As cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good tidings from a far country.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Proverbs 25:25, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: Two sorts of callings have appeared to me hard and dangerous: a merchant is hardly free from negligence: and a huckster shall not be justified from the sins of the lips.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.source: Ecclesiasticus 26:28, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: Let them that sail on the sea, tell the dangers thereof: and when we hear with our ears, we shall admire.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.when: when seamen tell their tales ashore
sayings.source: Ecclesiasticus 43:26, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: Today or tomorrow we will go into such a city, and there we will spend a year, and will traffic, and make our gain. Whereas you know not what shall be on the morrow.
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.when: to a merchant planning next year
sayings.source: James 4:13-14, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: What manner of man is this, for the winds and the sea obey him?
sayings.who: a priest or a monk
sayings.when: when the wind drops after prayer
sayings.source: Matthew 8:27, in the Douay-Rheims English (Challoner's revision, 1750) of the Latin Bible that the period's churchmen read

sayings.text: Three fingers write, and the whole body labours.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribes' closing note found in Latin books from the 8th century on ('Tres digiti scribunt, totum corpus laborat'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: As the harbour is welcome to sailors, so is the last line to the writer.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribes' closing note found in Latin books from the 8th century on ('Sicut portus oportunus navigantibus, ita versus novissimus scribentibus'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: He who cannot write thinks it no work.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribes' closing note found in Latin books from the 8th century on ('Qui scribere nescit nullum putat esse laborem'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Wash your hands before you take up the book; turn the leaves gently, and keep your finger well away from the letters.
sayings.who: a scribe or a keeper of books
sayings.when: when a seaman asks to see a book
sayings.source: A scribes' note to the reader in an 8th-century Latin law book ('lava manus tuas et sic librum adprehende, leniter folia turna, longe a littera digito pone'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: If anyone takes this book away, let him be cursed.
sayings.who: a scribe or a keeper of books
sayings.when: when a book is lent or carried
sayings.source: The usual curse written into church books against thieves ('Si quis abstulerit, anathema sit'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: If any man lessens this gift, let him know he must answer for it before God on the day of judgement.
sayings.who: a churchman reading out a charter
sayings.when: when a grant or a toll-freedom is read
sayings.source: The usual closing threat of 8th- and 9th-century English and Frankish charters; the game's own short telling of the formula (?)

sayings.text: Hail, star of the sea, kind mother of God.
sayings.who: a priest, a monk, a pious seaman
sayings.source: The hymn Ave maris stella, first found in a 9th-century book of St Gall ('Ave maris stella, Dei mater alma'); the game's own rendering; the date of the hymn's first use in the north is not checked (?)

sayings.text: What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed and when I am on horseback I cannot shield myself with them against wind and rain.
sayings.when: seeing the short Frisian cloaks for sale
sayings.source: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, Deeds of Charles the Great I.34: said by Charles when the Frisians sold short cloaks at the price of long ones, written 883-887; English of A. J. Grant (1907)

sayings.text: These ships are not filled with merchandise, but crowded with our fiercest enemies.
sayings.source: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, Deeds of Charles the Great II.14: said by Charles of the Northmen's ships, which he knew by their build and their speed, written 883-887; English of A. J. Grant (1907)

sayings.text: I am sad at heart to think that even during my lifetime they have dared to touch this shore.
sayings.who: an old Frank who remembers the great Charles
sayings.source: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, Deeds of Charles the Great II.14: part of what Charles said, weeping at the window, written 883-887; English of A. J. Grant (1907)

sayings.text: Would that our kings held gold and silver so cheap and iron so precious.
sayings.who: a Northman who has seen the Franks' court
sayings.source: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, Deeds of Charles the Great II.18: said by the Northmen's envoys, written 883-887; English of A. J. Grant (1907)

sayings.text: I have gone through this washing business here twenty times already, and I have been dressed in excellent clothes of perfect whiteness; but a sack like this is more fit for clodhoppers than for soldiers.
sayings.who: an old Dane, baptised more than once
sayings.when: at Easter, at a Frankish court or church
