sayings.source: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, Deeds of Charles the Great II.19: a Northman at the court of Louis the Pious, written 883-887; English of A. J. Grant (1907)

sayings.text: A fine price indeed for so precious an article! I had rather throw it into the sea than let any man have it at so cheap and shameful a price.
sayings.who: a merchant from the south, selling
sayings.source: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, Deeds of Charles the Great I.16: the merchant who sold a bishop a painted mouse, written 883-887; English of A. J. Grant (1907)

sayings.text: Oh the iron! Woe for the iron!
sayings.when: when the king's host comes in sight
sayings.source: Notker the Stammerer of St Gall, Deeds of Charles the Great II.17: the cry of the people of Pavia when they saw the host of Charles, written 883-887; English of A. J. Grant (1907)

sayings.text: When it rains, the trees get wet; when it blows, the trees shake.
sayings.when: rain; a man who states the plain
sayings.source: A proverb set down in Old High German by Notker the German of St Gall (d. 1022) in his schoolbook on logic ('Sô iz regenôt, sô nazzênt tî boumâ; sô iz uuât, sô uuagônt tî boumâ'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: You cannot make two sons-in-law with one daughter.
sayings.when: of a man who has promised one cargo twice
sayings.source: A proverb set down in Old High German by Notker the German of St Gall (d. 1022) in his schoolbook on logic; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: When the little roebuck runs, his rump shows white.
sayings.when: of a man seen running from a fight or a debt
sayings.source: A proverb set down in Old High German by Notker the German of St Gall (d. 1022) in his schoolbook on logic; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: If you are ill, then you are not well.
sayings.source: A proverb set down in Old High German by Notker the German of St Gall (d. 1022) in his schoolbook on logic; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: From the strap the dog learns to eat leather.
sayings.source: A proverb set down in Old High German by Notker the German of St Gall (d. 1022) in his schoolbook on logic; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: What is there between a sot and a Scot? Only the table.
sayings.when: at table, a Frank and an Irishman drinking
sayings.source: The jest of King Charles the Bald and John the Irishman at table, c. 850, told by William of Malmesbury in the 12th century ('Quid distat inter sottum et Scottum? Tabula tantum'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: I forsake all the devil's works and words, Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot and all the fiends that are their companions.
sayings.who: a newly baptised man
sayings.source: The Old Saxon baptismal vow, late 8th century; the chest's own draft from the original (texts_793.json, saxon_vow)

sayings.text: Bone to bone, blood to blood, limb to limb, as if they were glued.
sayings.who: a healer who keeps the old words
sayings.when: a sprain or a broken limb
sayings.source: The second Merseburg charm, Old High German, written down in the 10th century ('ben zi bena, bluot zi bluoda, lid zi geliden, sose gelimida sin'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Leap out of the bonds; get away from the enemy.
sayings.who: a healer who keeps the old words
sayings.source: The first Merseburg charm, Old High German, written down in the 10th century ('insprinc haptbandun, inuar uigandun'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Go out, worm, with your nine little worms: out of the marrow into the bone, out of the bone into the flesh, out of the flesh into the skin, out of the skin into this arrow.
sayings.who: a healer who keeps the old words
sayings.when: for a sick man or a sick horse
sayings.source: The Old Saxon charm against worms, written down in the 10th century ('Gang ut, nesso, mid nigun nessiklinon'); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Then the weather's strength began: the storm rose, the waves grew, darkness swung down among them; the sea was stirred up, and wind and water fought.
sayings.who: a singer of the Gospel in Saxon
sayings.source: Heliand, c. 830-840, fitt 27: the storm on the lake of Galilee, told as a storm on a northern sea; the game's own rendering from the Old Saxon as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: We Frisians need march no further than the Weser on the one side and the Fli on the other, for we must hold our land against the salt sea and against the wild wicing.
sayings.source: The Frisian Seventeen Statutes, statute 10, in 13th-century books of older law; told later; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Some of us who on various occasions have been to Dorstadt have of our own accord adopted this form of religion, believing it to be beneficial. Our way thither is now beset by those who lie in wait for us and is rendered dangerous by the attacks of pirates.
sayings.who: a trader of Birka, at the assembly
sayings.when: talk of the road to Dorestad
sayings.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, ch. 27: an old man speaks at the assembly of Birka, c. 852, written c. 870; English of C. H. Robinson (1921)

sayings.text: For, inasmuch as we cannot be sure that our gods will be favourably disposed, it is good for us to have the help of this God who is always, and under all circumstances able and willing to succour those who cry to Him.
sayings.who: a trader of Birka
sayings.when: asked which god he prays to
sayings.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, ch. 27: an old man speaks at the assembly of Birka, c. 852, written c. 870; English of C. H. Robinson (1921)

sayings.text: See, rain is at hand; call upon the names of your gods and ask that no rain fall upon you, and I will ask my Lord Jesus Christ that not a drop of rain may touch me.
sayings.who: a baptised man among heathen neighbours
sayings.when: rain coming on at an open-air meeting
sayings.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, ch. 19: Herigar, the prefect of Birka, to the men who mocked his faith (shortened), written c. 870; English of C. H. Robinson (1921)

sayings.text: Go with the money to Dorstadt. There are there many churches, priests, and clergy, and a multitude of poor people.
sayings.who: a Christian widow of Birka
sayings.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, ch. 20: the dying Frideburg to her daughter Catla, written c. 870; English of C. H. Robinson (1921)

sayings.text: A blessing on the soul of Fergus. Amen. I am very cold.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 114), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: It is dark to me.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 165), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: Alas! my hand.
sayings.who: a scribe; a man at the oar
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 176), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: New parchment, bad ink. O I say nothing more.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.when: handed bad tools or bad goods
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 217), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: The ink is thin.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 248), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: The parchment is scanty.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 228), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: This page has not been written very slowly.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 195), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: Love remains as long as property remains, O Maellecan.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.when: of a friend who cooled when the silver went
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 203), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: We are from Inis Maddoc, to wit, Coirbbre and I.
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 194), written in Ireland c. 850; English of W. Stokes and J. Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903)

sayings.text: Let whoever reads this sweat: it is a hard page.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 209: 'sudet qui legat, difficilis est ista pagina'), written in Ireland c. 850, as printed by Stokes and Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: It is time for dinner.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 228: 'tempus est prandii'), written in Ireland c. 850, as printed by Stokes and Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Night is here.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 246: 'nox adest'), written in Ireland c. 850, as printed by Stokes and Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Ale-sick.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 204, in ogham: 'latheirt', which Strachan took to be the word for the sickness after drink (?)), written in Ireland c. 850, as printed by Stokes and Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Saint Brigit, help the writer of this book.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: A scribe's note in the margin of the St Gall Priscian (Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. 904, p. 192: 'sancta brigita adiuua scriptorem istius artis'), written in Ireland c. 850, as printed by Stokes and Strachan, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903); the game's own rendering

sayings.text:
Bitter is the wind to-night,
It tosses the ocean's white hair:
To-night I fear not the fierce warriors of Norway
Coursing on the Irish Sea.
sayings.who: a monk on a coast
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'The Viking Terror', a quatrain in the margin of the St Gall Priscian, c. 850

sayings.text:
A hedge of trees surrounds me,
A blackbird's lay sings to me;
Above my lined booklet
The trilling birds chant to me.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'The Scribe', a quatrain in the margin of the St Gall Priscian, c. 850

sayings.text:
To go to Rome
Is much of trouble, little of profit:
The King whom thou seekest here,
Unless thou bring Him with thee, thou wilt not find.
sayings.who: a monk
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'The Pilgrim at Rome', 9th century; the 'thou' is Meyer's

sayings.text:
My tidings for you: the stag bells,
Winter snows, summer is gone.
Wind high and cold, low the sun,
Short his course, sea running high.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Summer is gone', 9th century (the first half)

sayings.text:
Deep-red the bracken, its shape all gone--
The wild-goose has raised his wonted cry.
Cold has caught the wings of birds;
Season of ice--these are my tidings.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Summer is gone', 9th century (the second half)

sayings.text:
Summer has come, healthy and free,
Whence the brown wood is aslope;
The slender nimble deer leap,
And the path of seals is smooth.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Summer has come', 10th century (the first quatrain)

sayings.text:
The blackbird sings a loud strain,
To him the live wood is a heritage,
The sad angry sea is fallen asleep,
The speckled salmon leaps.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Summer has come', 10th century (the sixth quatrain)

sayings.text:
Cold, cold!
Cold to-night is broad Moylurg,
Higher the snow than the mountain-range,
The deer cannot get at their food.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'A Song of Winter', 10th century (the first quatrain)

sayings.text:
A great tempest rages on the Plain of Ler, bold across its high borders
Wind has arisen, fierce winter has slain us; it has come across the sea,
It has pierced us like a spear.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Song of the Sea', 11th century (the first verse)

sayings.text:
The ocean is in flood, the sea is full, delightful is the home of ships,
The wind whirls the sand around the estuary,
Swiftly the rudder cleaves the broad sea.
sayings.when: a fair wind and a full tide
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Song of the Sea', 11th century

sayings.text:
Son of the God the Father, with mighty hosts, save me from the horror of fierce tempests!
Righteous Lord of the Feast, only save me from the horrid blast,
From Hell with furious tempest!
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Song of the Sea', 11th century (the last verse)

sayings.text:
I arise to-day
Through the strength of heaven:
Light of sun,
Radiance of moon,
Splendour of fire,
Speed of lightning,
Swiftness of wind,
Depth of sea,
Stability of earth,
Firmness of rock.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'The Deer's Cry', the hymn called Patrick's breastplate, not earlier than the 8th century

sayings.text:
Christ to shield me to-day
Against poison, against burning,
Against drowning, against wounding,
So that there may come to me abundance of reward.
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'The Deer's Cry', the hymn called Patrick's breastplate, not earlier than the 8th century

sayings.text:
I and my white Pangur
Have each his special art:
His mind is set on hunting mice,
Mine is upon my special craft.
sayings.who: a monk with a cat
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'The Monk and his Pet Cat', late 8th or early 9th century (the first quatrain)

sayings.text:
My hand is weary with writing,
My sharp quill is not steady,
My slender-beaked pen juts forth
A black draught of shining dark-blue ink.
sayings.who: a scribe
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Colum Cille the Scribe', probably 11th century (the first quatrain)

sayings.text:
O King of stars!
Whether my house be dark or bright,
Never shall it be closed against any one,
Lest Christ close His house against me.
sayings.who: a host
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Hospitality'

sayings.text:
When I am among my elders
I am proof that sport is forbidden:
When I am among the mad young folk
They think that I am their junior.
sayings.who: a man neither young nor old
sayings.source: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911): 'Moling sang this'

sayings.text: The three worst welcomes: a handicraft in the same house with the inmates; scalding water upon your feet; salt food without a drink.
sayings.when: salt food and no ale aboard
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three slender things that best support the world: the slender stream of milk from the cow's dug into the pail; the slender blade of green corn upon the ground; the slender thread over the hand of a skilled woman.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three rejoicings followed by sorrow: a wooer's, a thief's, a tale-bearer's.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three fewnesses that are better than plenty: a fewness of fine words; a fewness of cows in grass; a fewness of friends around good ale.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three laughing-stocks of the world: an angry man, a jealous man, a niggard.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three signs of ill-breeding: a long visit, staring, constant questioning.
sayings.when: of a guest who stays and asks
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three nurses of theft: a wood, a cloak, night.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three false sisters: 'perhaps,' 'may be,' 'I dare say.'
sayings.when: when a debtor will not name a day
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three timid brothers: 'hush!' 'stop!' 'listen!'
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three sounds of increase: the lowing of a cow in milk; the din of a smithy; the swish of a plough.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three keys that unlock thoughts: drunkenness, trustfulness, love.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: Three coffers whose depth is not known: the coffers of a chieftain, of the Church, of a privileged poet.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, gathered towards the end of the 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1906; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text:
Be not too wise, nor too foolish,
be not too conceited, nor too diffident,
be not too haughty, nor too humble,
be not too talkative, nor too silent,
be not too hard, nor too feeble.
sayings.source: The Instructions of King Cormac, early 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1909; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)
The Instructions of King Cormac, early 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1909; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911): the last four lines of his answer

sayings.text:
I was a listener in woods,
I was a gazer at stars,
I was blind where secrets were concerned,
I was silent in a wilderness,
I was talkative among many,
I was mild in the mead-hall,
I was stern in battle,
sayings.who: an old man, of his youth
sayings.source: The Instructions of King Cormac, early 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1909; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911): the first seven lines of his answer

sayings.text:
Music in moderation,
Short story-telling,
A joyous countenance,
Welcome to guests,
Silence during recitals,
Harmonious choruses.
sayings.when: of what an ale-house owes its guests
sayings.source: The Instructions of King Cormac, early 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1909; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911): the end of his answer on the dues of a chief and of an ale-house

sayings.text: rising too early, cold, sun, hunger, drinking too much, eating too much, sleeping too much, sinning too much, grief, running up a height, shouting against the wind
sayings.when: of what is worst for a man's body
sayings.source: The Instructions of King Cormac, early 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1909; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911): part of his list of what is worst for the body

sayings.text:
The shout of triumph after victory,
Praise after wages,
A lady's invitation to her pillow.
sayings.when: asked the sweetest thing he has heard
sayings.source: The Instructions of King Cormac, early 9th century; English of Kuno Meyer (1909; in his Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911)

sayings.text: The wind from the east is purple, from the south white, from the north black, from the west dun.
sayings.source: After the coloured winds of Saltair na Rann, late 10th century; the game's own short telling (?)

sayings.text: Who is the huge one, who passes over the earth, swallowing water and woods; he fears the wind, but no man, and wages war on the sun?
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 5 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: Who is the big one, who wades in the deep, turning half towards Hell; he saves people, but tugs against the earth, if he has a trusty withy by him?
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 6 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: Who are the maids that go weeping to the joy of their father, white-hooded, fair-haired, wide awake in a gale?
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 21 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: Who are the brides that walk over the reefs, and drive along the friths; these white-hooded ladies have a hard bed; in calm weather they make no stir?
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 23 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: What drink was it I drank yesterday; it was neither wine nor water, nor mead, nor beer, nor aught of meat kind; yet I went thirstless away?
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 3 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: I came from home, I wended my way from home, I saw a way of ways; way underneath, way above head, way on all sides.
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 2 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: Who are the maids that fight weaponless around their lord; the brown ever sheltering, the fair ever attacking him?
sayings.answer: The pieces of the board game.
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 19 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: Four ganging, four hanging, two showing the way, two keeping the dogs off, one ever dirty lags behind.
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 28 in Hervarar saga, written down in the 13th century; English of G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883), the refrain left off

sayings.text: Thor hallow these runes.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.when: naming a boat; setting up a stone
sayings.source: The Glavendrup stone, Funen, early 10th century (DR 209: 'Þur uiki þasi runar'); the game's own rendering

sayings.text: A warlock be he who harms this stone or drags it off to stand for another.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.when: of a boundary stone, a grave or a marked stake
sayings.source: The Glavendrup stone, Funen, early 10th century (DR 209: 'At rita sa uarþi is stain þansi ailti iþa aft anan traki'); the game's own rendering, the meaning of 'rita' uncertain (?)

sayings.text: They went like men, far for gold, and in the east they fed the eagle. They died in the south, in Serkland.
sayings.when: of the men who went east with Ingvar
sayings.source: The Gripsholm stone, Södermanland, c. 1040 (Sö 179); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Ulf has taken three gelds in England. The first was the one Tosti paid. Then Thorkel paid. Then Knut paid.
sayings.source: The Yttergärde stone, Uppland, c. 1020-1050 (U 344, in runes_793.json as yttergarde_u344); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: King Harald had this monument made for Gorm his father and Thyra his mother: the Harald who won all Denmark for himself, and Norway, and made the Danes Christian.
sayings.when: of the king's stone at Jelling
sayings.source: The great Jelling stone, c. 965 (DR 42); the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: With law shall the land be built up, and with lawlessness laid waste.
sayings.source: Njáls saga ch. 70 and the Frostathing law ('Með lögum skal land byggja'); written down in the 13th century of older law; the game's own rendering

sayings.text: Bare is the back of the man who has no brother.
sayings.when: of a man with no kin aboard
sayings.source: Grettis saga ch. 82 and Njáls saga ch. 152 ('Berr er hverr á bakinu nema sér bróður eigi'); written down in the 13th and 14th centuries; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Ale is another man.
sayings.source: Grettis saga ch. 19 ('Öl er annarr maðr'); written down in the 14th century; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: A tale is half told when one man tells it.
sayings.when: hearing one side of a quarrel
sayings.source: Grettis saga ch. 46; written down in the 14th century; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Only a thrall takes his revenge at once, and a coward never.
sayings.source: Grettis saga ch. 15; written down in the 14th century; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: He is not to blame who gives the warning.
sayings.source: Njáls saga ch. 41 ('Eigi veldr sá er varar'); written down in the 13th century; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: My mother said they should buy me a boat and fair oars, to go off with the wicings, to stand up in the stem and steer a dear ship, to hold on for harbour and cut down a man or two.
sayings.who: a boy who wants to go to sea
sayings.source: The verse given to the boy Egil in Egils saga ch. 40 ('Þat mælti mín móðir'); written down in the 13th century of c. 917; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Trolls take you.
sayings.source: The common curse of the sagas ('Troll hafi þik'); written down in the 13th century; the game's own rendering

sayings.text: O my lord, I have come from a far country with so many slave girls and so many sable skins. Send me a merchant with many gold and silver coins, who will buy from me as I wish and not argue with what I say.
sayings.who: a trader on the eastern rivers, before his gods
sayings.when: setting out his goods at a market
sayings.source: After Ibn Fadlan's account of the Rus traders on the Volga, 922: the prayer before the wooden post; the game's own telling of it, not a translation (?)

sayings.text: Wulfstan said that he went from Haddeby,—that he was in Truso in seven days and nights,—that the ship was running all the way under sail.
sayings.source: Wulfstan's voyage in the Old English Orosius, c. 890; English of J. Bosworth (1859), as in the chest

sayings.text: Ohthere said that the district in which he dwelt was called Halgoland. He said that no man abode north of him.
sayings.source: Ohthere's account in the Old English Orosius, c. 890; English of J. Bosworth (1859), as in the chest

sayings.text: Thither he said, that a man could not sail in a month, if he anchored at night, and every day had a fair wind.
sayings.when: talk of the long coast of Norway
sayings.source: Ohthere's account in the Old English Orosius, c. 890, of the way to Sciringesheal; English of J. Bosworth (1859), as in the chest

sayings.text: Among the Este the king and the richest men drink mare's milk, and the poor and the slaves drink mead. No ale is brewed there, but there is mead enough.
sayings.when: talk of Truso and the Este
sayings.source: After Wulfstan's account of the Este in the Old English Orosius, c. 890; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: There is a people among the Este who can make cold. Set down two tubs of ale or water, and they will have both frozen over, summer or winter.
sayings.when: talk of Truso and the Este
sayings.source: After Wulfstan's account of the Este in the Old English Orosius, c. 890; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: A ring round the moon: wind or rain before the second night.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the sign is a true one

sayings.text: A sky like a mackerel's back: the wind will shift before two tides are out.
sayings.when: a sky of small rippled cloud
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the sign is a true one

sayings.text: Gulls sitting on the ploughland: leave the boat where she lies.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Porpoises playing round the stem: look for wind from where they came.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A swell with no wind is yesterday's storm or tomorrow's.
sayings.when: a long swell in a calm
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the sign is a true one

sayings.text: An east wind in spring is dry, cold and honest. A south-wester is warm, wet and a liar.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Fog that comes in with the flood goes out with the ebb, unless it likes you.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: When you can count the trees on the far shore, it will rain before night.
sayings.when: the far shore sharp and near
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the sign is a true one

sayings.text: If the wind goes round with the sun it will hold fair. If it goes against the sun it will be back, and harder.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the sign is a true one in these seas

sayings.text: Dew on the thwarts at dawn: a dry day.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Rain before wind: get the sail down. Wind before rain: you may soon set it again.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after a later seamen's rule

sayings.text: When the smoke of the salt-fires lies along the ground, the rain is on its way.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; salt was burnt from peat on the Frisian coast

sayings.text: Stars that flicker hard mean wind by morning.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: After the winter nights only fools and kings' men are at sea.
sayings.when: the end of the sailing year
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Northmen counted winter from the winter nights, about the middle of the tenth month

sayings.text: From Martinmas to Candlemas the sea belongs to God, and He does not lend it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Martinmas is the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Candlemas the second day of the second

sayings.text: New moon and full moon bring the big tides. The man who forgets it sits on the sand until the next.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Bede had written on the moon and the tides in 725

sayings.text: Watch the wave that comes after the big one. If a bigger follows, the wind is rising.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: When the wild geese come early, lay in wood.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Much herring, much wind.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: When the water burns in the oar-strokes at night, look for a change.
sayings.when: a dark night, the water glowing at the oars
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: When the sun lets down his ropes to draw water, he pours it back tomorrow.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A low dawn is a fair day. A high dawn, over a bank of cloud, is wind.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after a later seamen's rule

sayings.text: Hang a strip of sea-tangle by the door: limp for rain, hard for fair.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: When the ice sings at night it will bear a horse by morning.
sayings.when: hard frost on the east sea
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A north wind is a hard master but an honest one: it shows you every rock.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The east sea freezes from the bays outward. Be out of the bays before the birches are bare.
sayings.when: the end of the sailing year on the east sea
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: On the shoals, trust the pole before your eyes: the sand moved last winter and told no one.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A wet Lammas, a dear loaf.
sayings.when: the feast of the first loaf
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Lammas, the loaf-mass, is the first day of the eighth month

sayings.text: A wet vintage makes thin wine, and thin wine travels badly.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A red sun going down into a clear sea: sleep. A pale sun going down into a wall: sleep in turns.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: When the gannets fish close under the land, the weather is coming out of the west.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Frost on Saint Peter's Chair holds the ice another forty nights.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the feast of Saint Peter's Chair is the 22nd day of the second month; later weather sayings hang on it

sayings.text: When the cranes go over, mend your sail. When the swallows go, mend your roof.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: My knee says the wind is going round. My knee has been at sea longer than you have.
sayings.who: an old hand
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A tenth here, a tenth at Quentovic, and they wonder that a man goes in by the back creeks.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the king's toll at Dorestad and Quentovic was a tenth

sayings.text: The king's new penny is heavier, they say. Mine buy no more than the old ones did.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the heavier penny ordered at Frankfurt in 794

sayings.text: The moneyer takes his share for turning good silver into the king's face. I liked the silver well enough before.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Every port has its own pound, and every one of them is lighter when you sell than when you buy.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Three days of salt fish and the ale gone sour. If the wind does not change, the crew will.
sayings.when: days at sea, the ale gone
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: She leaks a bucket an hour. I have counted them; I had nothing else to do.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Wet bread, wet wool, wet feet. The sea is in everything but the cup.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Forty days of herring, and when it ends they give you an egg and call it a feast.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Pitch has gone up again. The pines must be dying of pride.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: We wait for the tide, then for the wind, then for the toll man. The toll man is the slowest of the three.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The reeve wants to witness every sale. A man cannot sell an egg in this town without a king's man watching.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the laws of the Kentish kings ask that a sale in London be made before the king's reeve or good witnesses

sayings.text: The river has moved again. One day we will sail up to Dorestad and find it has gone to live somewhere else.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Rhine at Dorestad was shifting and silting in these years

sayings.text: The count takes the toll, the bishop takes the tithe, the abbot takes the best field. The king takes the count, the bishop and the abbot to war.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: First they took our gods, then a tenth of our corn. I miss the corn more.
sayings.who: an old Saxon, baptised by order
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the tithe laid on the newly baptised Saxons by Charles

sayings.text: Porters. They carry half, drop a third, and want ale for the rest.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A lodging with fleas, a host with long ears, and ale like the ditch. I have paid for all three.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The wind is always fair for the ship going the other way.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The Franks buy our cloth by the ell, and measure the ell with a longer arm each year.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The Saxons want salt, the Danes want slaves, the Franks want tribute. Nobody wants to be left alone as much as we do.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A mark of silver here is not a mark at home. I carry my own weights, and nobody trusts those either.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: There is no book in this port that is not a toll-book. I would give my cloak for a psalter with all its leaves.
sayings.who: a monk far from his minster
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: They call it ale. In my country we would wash the dog in it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Fog. You pay a pilot to tell you that he cannot see either.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Winter. The boat is on the bank, the silver is in the count's chest, and my wife's mother is in my house.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Since the heathen men came to the holy island, every sail on this coast is counted twice and trusted once.
sayings.when: a strange sail on the coast
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the raid on Lindisfarne in 793

sayings.text: The king has his toll at both ends of the road across the neck. A man now pays to leave one sea and pays again to reach the other.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; King Godfred brought the merchants of Reric to Sliesthorp in 808; the double toll is a guess (?)

sayings.text: A Frisian will sell you half a cloak and tell you the other half is the fashion.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after Notker's tale of the short Frisian cloaks

sayings.text: A Frank tells you his king's name before he tells you his own.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: It blew a little.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: We lost the mast and two oars. Apart from that it was a quiet crossing.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Count it again. I know you counted it twice. Twice only tells me that you can count.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A Svea counts his silver twice and your fingers once.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: They baptised me in the river in winter. The water was cold enough to make a believer of any man.
sayings.who: an old Saxon, baptised by order
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the baptisms of the Saxon wars

sayings.text: A Wend swears by the water. A Saxon swears by the saints. Watch the man who swears by both.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Wendish oath on water is not checked (?)

sayings.text: How do you know the tide is out? The Frank is aground.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Ask a Frisian the price and he asks what you have. Ask him the weather and he asks what you will pay.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The steersman is always right. When he is wrong the sea tells him, not you.
sayings.when: of the man at the steering oar
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: My father said: never lend a boat, a wife or a whetstone. He lent all three and got the whetstone back.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The abbot fasts on fish. It is a hard rule: the fish must be fresh, and there must be wine with it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The Franks have built a tower to watch for us. It is kind of them: now we can see where the town is.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Charles set watches and ships on his coasts from 800

sayings.text: The best steersmen stand on the shore.
sayings.when: when a man on the quay gives advice
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; a Dutch proverb of later centuries says the same

sayings.text: He rowed so hard that we only went round twice.
sayings.when: of a new man at the oar
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: To the knee, if you are a heron.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: We sell the Danes the wine, the Svear the jars, and the English the story of how good it was.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Hang the hammer and the cross on the same string. Somebody is listening.
sayings.when: of a man with two amulets
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I eat a tenth of everything and am never fat. I stand at every quay. Kings feed on what I leave.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I was a tree. Now I walk on water with one wing and many legs, and carry my masters in my belly.
sayings.answer: A ship under sail and oars.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the ship riddles of the Latin and English riddlers

sayings.text: Twice a day I come to the door, and twice I go away. I take what is left on the step.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have a king's head and no body. I buy a man's bread, and I am cut to prove me true.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; silver was nicked with a knife to test it

sayings.text: Born of the sea and the fire, I die in water. Kings take a share of me, and without me the fish stinks.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I owe nothing, yet I am notched for every debt. Split me, and each half tells the same tale.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The more of me you throw out, the more comes in. Leave me alone and I leave you nothing.
sayings.answer: The water in the bottom of the boat.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Black stones that came down the river and now go round all day without going anywhere, eating corn and giving flour.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I bite iron and grow thinner for it. A man carries me at his belt, and I came further than he did.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the grey whetstones came from Norway

sayings.text: I have one wing and no feathers. I carry the house that carries me. When I am full, there is nothing in me.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Dry feet and a full hold.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Fair wind and whole planks.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Saint Willibrord keep your keel.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Willibrord (d. 739), the apostle of the Frisians

sayings.text: Saint Martin share his cloak with you this winter.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Saint Cuthbert quiet the sea for you, as he did for the monks on the rafts.
sayings.when: before a passage on the north coast
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Bede's Life of Cuthbert, ch. 3, tells how the boy's prayer turned the wind for monks adrift on the Tyne

sayings.text: Brendan's luck to you: a long voyage and a landfall at the end of it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the voyage of Saint Brendan was being told in these years (?)

sayings.text: Colum Cille's blessing on the boat and on everyone in her.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Thor keep the weather off you.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Njord give you wind, and Frey a buyer.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Njord rules the wind and the sea and Frey gives plenty, as Snorri tells in the 13th century (?)

sayings.text: Pour the first ale over the stem before you drink any. The boat was thirsty first.
sayings.who: a man of the old ways
sayings.when: the first ale of a voyage
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May the water carry you as it carries an oath.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Wendish oath on water is not checked (?)

sayings.text: Perkun strike beside you and not on you.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the thunder god of the Balts, named only in later sources (?)

sayings.text: God send you a soft wind, a short passage and an honest toll man. Two of the three would do.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: God and the king's peace go with you as far as the river mouth. After that, God alone.
sayings.when: at parting, in a Frankish port
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: God bring you home with your goods, or with your life, or with both.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Bless the bread, the ale and the hands that row.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Light the midsummer fire high. The boats at sea should see where home is.
sayings.when: the feast of Saint John at midsummer
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; fires on Saint John's night are an old custom the bishops preached against (?)

sayings.text: Holy Olaf hold his hand over us.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; King Olaf fell at Stiklestad in 1030 and was held a saint within the year

sayings.text: May your planks open at the first wave.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May the worm have your keel and the toll man your cargo.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May you row home against wind and tide both.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May your ale turn and your wife learn to count.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May the sea remember where you live.
sayings.when: of a man who has cheated a neighbour
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Ran take you and Hel keep you.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Ran with her net and Hel with her hall are told of in the 13th century (?)

sayings.text: May he sit with Judas at the low end of the table.
sayings.who: a churchman
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the curses that close the period's charters

sayings.text: May he be seven years on the sea and never sight a land that wants him.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May his sail hang slack while his enemies row.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May the river turn its back on him.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May his silver be found by a stranger's plough.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; silver was hidden in the ground, and much of it never dug up again

sayings.text: May he buy dear, sell cheap, and be thanked for it.
sayings.who: a merchant
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May the tithe-man find his barn before he does.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: May the Northmen come to his door first and to mine not at all.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the Danish fleet that fell on Frisia in 810

sayings.text: A head wind to him, all the way.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: We stand on ground our fathers carried here in baskets.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Frisians raised their dwelling mounds above the tide

sayings.text: I have paid toll in six tongues and been cheated in all of them. I count that as learning.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: This boat has touched bottom in every river from the Seine to the Eider, and only twice by mistake.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have been to Birka and home again between the hay and the harvest.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have rowed a little.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have weighed silver that came from Serkland, with letters on it that no priest can read.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the silver coins of the caliphs reached the east sea from about 800

sayings.text: I have been where the sun does not set at midsummer, and a man can mend a net at midnight.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I carried six books over the sea for a bishop, and the sea did not read a line of them.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have seen King Charles ride into Nijmegen. The horses alone would have bought this town.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the palace at Nijmegen was one of the houses of Charles the Great

sayings.text: My father sold cloth to King Offa's reeve and came home with his ears and his silver both.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the quarrel of Charles and Offa, c. 790, when the ports were shut to each other's merchants

sayings.text: My ship sits so light that she leaves the water dry behind her.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have crossed in a boat of hides sewn with thong, and it was drier than your oak.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: No toll man has ever found what I did not want him to find.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have been wrecked twice. The sea has had two chances at me and wasted both.
sayings.who: an old hand
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: On Gotland every farmer is a merchant, and every merchant has a farm to go home to. Who else can say that?
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I can smell a sandbank in the dark.
sayings.who: a pilot
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Our amber lies on the beach for the picking. You cross the sea for what our children play with.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: I have carried a boat on my shoulders from one river to the next, and paid men to say it was a road.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The sea gives back what it takes, but not to the same man.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: News is like fish: buy it fresh or do not buy it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A price is as old as the ship that brought it.
sayings.when: hearing a price from another port
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Buy where they make it, sell where they miss it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A good king is one whose pennies weigh the same two years running.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The man who talks about the storm was not in the worst of it.
sayings.when: when a man tells of a storm
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Trust the scales, then the man. If you must choose, the scales.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Silver in the ground does not rust and does not quarrel.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: An oath on water runs away if you break it, and takes your luck with it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Wendish oath on water is not checked (?)

sayings.text: Better a small boat of your own than an oar in a great one.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A debt sails with you, even when the lender stays ashore.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: One hand for the boat and one for yourself.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after a later seamen's rule

sayings.text: Days are the only cargo you cannot buy more of.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The sea does not know who is a bishop.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Wine remembers the cask, and a buyer remembers the wine.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The river is long, but the fur is light.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Do not praise the harbour until you have seen the toll.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A sandbank is the only thing on this coast that comes to meet you.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Feed the crew before you feed the gods. The gods can wait, and they cannot row.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Keep a piece of silver on you at sea. If Ran takes you, do not come to her hall with empty hands.
sayings.who: a man of the old gods
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the sagas, written later, tell of men carrying gold for Ran (?)

sayings.text: If I break this, may I be cursed by Perun and by Volos the god of cattle, turn yellow as gold, and be cut down by my own weapons.
sayings.who: a trader of the eastern rivers, swearing to a bargain
sayings.source: After the oaths of the Rus in their treaties with the Greeks (907, 945, 971) as the Primary Chronicle of c. 1113 gives them; told later; the game's own telling, not a translation (?)

sayings.text: A squirrel skin is small money, a marten good money, a sable a king's money.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; furs passed as money on the eastern rivers (?)

sayings.text: The rapids take one boat in ten, and the tribute-takers one skin in ten. I am less afraid of the rapids.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Among the Este a dead man's goods are laid out along the road in heaps, and the man with the fastest horse rides off with the largest.
sayings.when: talk of Truso and the Este
sayings.source: After Wulfstan's account of the Este in the Old English Orosius, c. 890; the game's own telling as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: The man who brings salt is welcome twice: once when he comes, and once when he says he will come back.
sayings.when: when a salt ship comes in
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: After a north-west gale, be on the beach before your neighbour: the sea pays in amber.
sayings.when: the morning after a gale from the north-west
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; amber is thrown up on the south shore of the east sea after storms

sayings.text: The Franks call us allies when the Saxons are restless, and heathens when they are quiet.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Obodrites fought beside Charles against the Saxons

sayings.text: Reric is burnt, and its merchants were driven off to Sliesthorp like cattle to a new field.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; King Godfred destroyed Reric in 808 and took its merchants to Sliesthorp

sayings.text: Our rivers are so full of fish that a spear stuck in the water stands up by itself.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the praise of the Wendish land's plenty in the 12th-century Lives of Otto of Bamberg (?)

sayings.text: Honey, wax and furs go out; salt and iron come in. Whoever stands in the doorway grows rich.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Salt from the Bay, wine from the Garonne. God made this coast for merchants.
sayings.when: on the coast of the Bay
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: The monks of Saint Philibert leave their island every spring now, and come back when the Northmen have gone home.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the monks of Noirmoutier fled the raids each summer from 819 and left for good in 836

sayings.text: A Saxon gives his word once. The Franks made us give ours every spring.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; after the oaths and risings of the Saxon wars, 772-804

sayings.text: King Radbod stood with one foot in the font and asked where his fathers were. In hell, said the bishop. So he took his foot out again: he would rather be with the kings of the Frisians than in heaven with a few poor men.
sayings.who: an old Frisian who keeps to the old ways
sayings.source: After the Life of Saint Wulfram, written about 800, on King Radbod of the Frisians (d. 719); the game's own telling, not a translation (?)

sayings.text: Whoever breaks into a shrine and takes the holy things is led down to the sea, and on the sand that the tide covers his ears are slit, he is gelded, and he is given to the gods whose house he robbed.
sayings.who: an old Frisian who keeps to the old ways
sayings.when: passing a shrine of the old gods
sayings.source: The Law of the Frisians, written down c. 802, in its last added clause; the game's own rendering from the Latin as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: Gotland was first found by a man called Thielvar. In those days the island sank by day and rose by night. He was the first to bring fire to it, and it never sank again.
sayings.source: Guta saga, written down in the 13th century; told later; the game's own rendering as remembered, to check (?)

sayings.text: King Godfred says that Frisia and Saxony are his own provinces, and that he will soon come to Aachen, where the emperor keeps his court.
sayings.source: After Einhard, Life of Charles, ch. 14; the game's own telling, not a translation
